summary: Kemetis is a web-based health-monitoring platform designed to support astronaut health awareness during long-duration space missions. Spaceflight conditions such as microgravity, radiation, isolation, and confinement can affect several aspects of human health, making continuous awareness of physiological and behavioral changes important. Kemetis brings health indicators together in a central interface, helping users review information and observe potential changes through visual data presentation. The project is informed by NASA human-spaceflight research on risks to astronaut health. Our goal is to develop a clearer, more accessible way to organize and interpret health information, supporting informed monitoring when immediate medical assistance may be limited.
details:
Kemetis is a web-based health-monitoring platform developed to address the physiological and behavioral health challenges astronauts may experience during long-duration space missions.

The platform is designed around the need to gather, organize, visualize, and interpret health indicators in a clear and accessible interface. Its dashboard-based approach allows users to observe health information, examine changes through dynamic charts, and receive alerts that draw attention to potential concerns.

The project focuses on supporting astronaut awareness of their health status and helping them recognize changes that may require further assessment. This is particularly relevant to deep-space missions, where communication delays and limited access to medical assistance increase the importance of onboard health awareness.

Development involved JavaScript, TypeScript, and Node.js. Google AI Studio was used to assist with code structure, Antigravity supported implementation and interface development, and Claude assisted with UI/UX development.

Kemetis is a software prototype intended to demonstrate how digital health-monitoring tools could support future human space exploration. It is not a clinically validated diagnostic system, and its outputs should not replace professional medical assessment.

Future development could include integration with validated physiological datasets, wearable health sensors, personalized baseline comparisons, more advanced anomaly detection, and additional behavioral-health monitoring capabilities.
